# Scribl Shape Kickoff / Prioritization Workshop -- Retro (2026-08-25)

Durable retro of the 2026-08-25 Scribl Shape kickoff / prioritization
workshop. Same exception as the 2026-07-14 kickoff retro: a workshop retro is
durable knowledge, not an operational record. The operational digest and the
action-item seam live at
[`knowledge/meetings/2026-08-25-scribl-shape-kickoff.md`](../../meetings/2026-08-25-scribl-shape-kickoff.md);
the raw transcript is preserved internally at
`knowledge/meetings/raw/2026-08-25-scribl-shape-kickoff.vtt` (not in the
rendered site).

**Format:** video call (Teams/Zoom mix per the small talk about "letting
external users in"), about one hour four minutes (first cue 00:00:03, last
cue ends 01:03:36). Facilitator: Rob Forshier II, who ran the whole agenda
solo and drove the screen share throughout.

| Side | People |
| --- | --- |
| Scribl | Eric Rice (CCO / game design), Matthew Kaplan (CEO) |
| Bounteous | Rob Forshier II (AI Architect, demo + facilitation) |

Only these three speak substantively in the transcript. The meeting digest
notes the invite list also included Martin Young, David Lawton, Angie Yap,
John Kilgore and Pramod Kumar; Martin Young has one one-word line ("Yap,"
00:04:56), Rob asks "Do you want to speak, Dave?" at 00:54:44 with no reply
recorded, and the rest of the invite list has no evidenced participation.
Treat that as unconfirmed attendance, not absence.

## How the workshop went

This was not a card-sorting prioritization session in the end. Rob opened by
saying the meeting was originally framed as feature-prioritization work but
that doesn't make sense yet: the epics and features were only just laid down,
and the backlog would not be in order until early-to-mid the following week
(00:02:49 to 00:03:16). What actually happened instead was a working session
in three parts: a full screen-by-screen walk of Rob's updated Vercel POC
built from Eric's latest wireframes, then Eric walking his own Figma feedback
board point by point against that POC, then Rob running the open-question set
on the shared Lucid board end to end.

The tone stayed collaborative and fast. Eric drove nearly every substantive
change request while live-reacting to the POC; Matthew pushed back twice,
both times on scope (the eraser/trash buttons, and iOS-only beta), and both
times the pushback was heard and recorded rather than steamrolled. Nothing
in this session was a formal vote; every decision below is Eric or Matthew
making a call in the room, sometimes over the other's stated objection.

Two staffing and delivery items opened the meeting before the demo: the lead
iOS engineer has a family emergency this week and part of next, dropped to
30 percent, with a replacement engineer starting onboarding the same day
(Rob, 00:03:49 to 00:04:24); and the team, three days in, picked React
Native with Expo as the stack, the same framework the POC itself is built
on (Rob, 00:48:38).

## Key learnings and shifts to carry forward

1. **The B2B game's feel, not its feature list, is the canvas acceptance
   bar.** Eric's real ask was to reproduce the "pushing paint around,
   finger-paint feeling" of the existing B2B canvas (00:21:10), and he
   unpacked that into four concrete asks: one brush, the eight colors, undo,
   and possibly an eraser (00:21:33). The canvas is done when it feels like
   the B2B game on a phone, not when a checklist of controls is present.
2. **Sharing was reframed mid-call from a screen into the product's
   center.** Eric: "this is actually a content creation platform and the
   ability for people to share this outwardly on their socials or via text
   or however is super, super important" (00:35:55). The MVP floor stays
   modest -- "at the very minimum, a static image, maybe there's room for
   text" (00:37:37) -- but the prompt appearing on the shared card is
   non-negotiable: "the prompt being featured is key so that people have
   context" (00:36:17).
3. **The POC does not currently store individual strokes, only the final
   flattened image**, and Rob found this out live while answering Eric's
   question about it (00:54:59). Eric's reasoning for wanting stroke data is
   concrete: he can already pull stored keystrokes for the B2B game out of
   Metabase and feed them to an LLM to reconstruct the drawing (00:56:05),
   and stroke replay opens future animation and GIF options. Rob's read is
   that a stroke is cheap to store (a color plus a start and end point,
   "literally just... a vector store," 00:56:57), which answers Eric's own
   stated worry about storage cost (00:56:34).
4. **iOS-only for the beta was reopened and re-decided in the room**, not
   assumed. Matthew argued a beta drawn only from iOS families excludes
   mixed-platform families like his own (00:50:48 to 00:51:19). Eric asked
   Rob directly to recommend (00:51:32); Rob proposed iOS as the engineering
   focus with best-effort free Android builds shipped alongside rather than
   a true iOS-only beta; Eric accepted it ("Let's do that," 00:52:20). See
   Decisions below -- this is a real re-decision with dissent on the record,
   not a rubber stamp of the earlier assumption.
5. **Christina's design scope is exactly three screens**, named twice in the
   session: the intro screen, the home screen, and the single-story
   shareable, which may carry into the Artifact treatment too (Eric,
   00:07:13, reconfirmed 00:28:51 and 00:36:17). Everything else is Rob
   replicating her established theme; Eric or Alex cover anything beyond
   that.
6. **Challenges came back into MVP scope, trimmed.** Rob had removed
   challenges from the POC believing they were cut. Eric wants them back for
   MVP, scoped down to injecting a new prompt only, triggered by a wall
   member picking from a family game pack (00:33:20 to 00:33:42), with the
   fuller "chance card" mechanic (restrict color, restrict hand, etc.)
   explicitly deferred (00:33:39 to 00:34:45).

Not decided, held open on the record:

- **Eraser.** Eric asked for it; Matthew objected there is no user data behind
  it; Eric took it to an internal Scribl conversation rather than deciding
  (00:23:38).
- **Exact brush width.** Eric picked "second from the right" off the
  desktop screen share; Matthew, holding a phone, said the third or fourth
  option looked closer to the current B2B line weight. Neither yielded
  (00:25:15 to 00:26:07).
- **Missed-day wall-unlock rule.** Rob's POC lets a user write an
  explanation to unlock a missed day retroactively. Matthew is uneasy with
  rewarding a broken streak (Wordle comparison, 00:31:42); Eric closed it as
  "the functionality... is there. We just need to figure out the exact...
  rule set for it," pending an internal Scribl conversation with Eric
  (00:29:35 to 00:32:59).

## What was demoed

Rob walked his updated Vercel POC live, built from Eric's latest wireframes
and using the same AWS backend and accounts as before (00:09:18 onward):
splash and sign-up with a new "always show onboarding" toggle for demo
purposes, the Scribl welcome and prompt-of-the-day screens (colors already
updated per Eric's morning note), the canvas (voice-or-text choice, single
cloud drawing demo), the personal wall with voice-note playback, wall
creation and comma-delimited email invites, a live two-account invite/accept
flow (Rob inviting his wife), themes trimmed to white plus a new dark mode,
and wall leave/delete/remove-member controls. The sharing feature was noted
as in progress during the call. After the POC walk, Eric ran his own Figma
feedback board point by point against what had just been shown (00:18:48
onward), which produced most of the canvas, home-screen, and sharing
decisions above.

## Open questions / future decisions

- AWS hosting: new instance vs. the existing B2B AWS account, and which is
  best practice -- unresolved; Rob to loop in Bounteous's AWS side and follow
  up with Scribl's contacts James and Bhasin (00:46:01 to 00:47:44).
- Apple developer accounts do not exist yet on Scribl's side; provisioning
  time is unknown even to Rob ("I've never built a mobile app," 01:02:36).
- Test management / QA software: Scribl does not know what it uses today;
  Matthew suggested routing the question to Nick (00:52:59 to 00:53:24).
- Crash analytics tool (Sentry vs. Firebase): left to Bounteous; Scribl has
  nothing today (00:57:29 to 00:57:56).
- Eraser decision, exact brush width, and the missed-day unlock rule set --
  see "Not decided" above.
- Artifact scope and timing beyond the manual long-press compose feature
  (AI-assisted composition, training corpus, monetization/token system) --
  explicitly banded later phase by Eric himself.

## Risks raised

- **Two open decisions have no date attached.** The eraser/white call and
  the missed-day reveal rule both went to "we'll talk about it internally"
  with no committed return date. If either slips past the next sprint
  boundary, the canvas and wall-unlock work get built against Rob's best
  guess instead of a client decision -- the same failure mode flagged in the
  2026-07-14 retro's "future and open decisions" list.
- **Stroke storage is not retroactive.** The gap Rob found live (POC only
  records the final image, not keystrokes) cannot be backfilled onto art
  already submitted, which makes fixing it urgent rather than a nice-to-have
  cleanup.
- **Two client voices, no reconciliation process.** The brush-width
  disagreement between Eric (desktop screen share) and Matthew (phone in
  hand) surfaced no mechanism for resolving device-dependent product calls;
  it was left as "finesse it once we start playing with it" (00:25:49).

## Where the transcript disagrees with the other records

Named here rather than silently resolved, so whoever reconciles the four
Eric records knows what they are walking into.

**Canvas color count: eight vs. nine.** `knowledge/client-feedback/2026-08-25-eric-screen-feedback.md`
(the written, emailed feedback) fixes the canvas at eight named colors and
treats "erase" as a possible interchangeable-with-white option, not a ninth
swatch. The transcript itself is not internally consistent on this count.
Early in the canvas walk, Eric confirms eight: "Moving over the canvas, you
got the new colors. We're going with those eight" (00:20:56). Later in the
same conversation, after Rob asks whether to add white, Eric says yes,
provisionally: "I think you know white and race would be interchangeable...
we'd probably just have you add a white option... There seems to be some
differences of opinion" (00:27:17), and Rob restates the count out loud:
"do you want me to add white? So technically it'll be 9 colors" (00:27:01).
**The transcript settles this to nine, provisionally** -- eight fixed colors
plus a ninth white swatch that Eric flagged as still contested inside
Scribl. The written feedback's "eight" predates this addition and should be
read as superseded, not as a second correct answer. `knowledge/client-feedback/2026-08-25-eric-spoken-feedback.md`
already carries this same amendment and reaches the same conclusion.

**Brush width: second-from-right vs. third/fourth.** Eric and Matthew never
converged on a specific brush size in the transcript (00:25:15 to 00:26:07,
detailed under "Not decided" above). Neither the digest nor the change-request
tracker resolves this to a single number either -- both correctly record it
as open. This page does the same rather than picking one.

**Board question count: ten vs. eleven rows.** The meeting digest notes the
Lucid board's open-question set nominally has ten questions, but the AWS
question splits into "do you have an environment" and "new instance or
existing, and what's best practice," so the digest's answer table runs to
eleven rows. This page's board-answer content matches the digest; it is
flagged here only so a reader comparing row counts between this page and the
digest is not confused by the split.
